title: Smallest Partner for OR With Next
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers. For each x = nums[i], find the smallest non-negative integer a such that a | (a + 1) === x, where | is bitwise OR.

Return an array of the same length holding that a for each position, or -1 where no such a exists.

examples.why: 3 | 4 = 011 | 100 = 111 = 7. 6 also works for 7 (110 | 111), but 3 is smaller. For 6 nothing works: a | (a + 1) is always odd. For 13 = 1101, 12 | 13 = 1101.
11 = 1011 and 9 | 10 = 1001 | 1010 = 1011. Just subtracting 1 gives 10, which is valid but not the smallest. For 1, a = 0 works since 0 | 1 = 1.
2 is even, so it is impossible. 31 = 11111, and 15 | 16 = 01111 | 10000 = 11111.

hints: Write a and a + 1 in binary. What does adding 1 do to the trailing 1s of a?

Adding 1 turns a's trailing run of 1s into 0s and the 0 just above them into a 1. OR-ing a with a + 1 therefore fills that 0 and keeps everything else. So x must end in a 1, and an even x is impossible.
For odd x, find the lowest 0 bit of x. The answer is x with the bit just below that 0 cleared, which is x − (lowest zero bit) / 2.

explain.intuition:
Adding 1 to a flips its trailing 1s to 0s and turns the next 0 into a 1. So a | (a + 1) is just a with its lowest 0 bit switched on. That gives two facts. The result always ends in 1, so even x has no answer. And a must be x with one bit of its trailing run of 1s turned off, the bit that becomes the "lowest 0".

x ends in a run of 1s. Turning off any bit inside that run works, and turning off the highest one of the run makes a smallest. If low is the lowest 0 bit of x, that is low / 2, so a = x − low / 2. A quick way to get low is (x + 1) & ~x.
steps: For each x: if x is even, the answer is -1.
Otherwise compute low = (x + 1) & ~x, the lowest 0 bit of x.
pitfalls: Answering x − 1. It is always valid for odd x, but only the smallest when x ends in a single 1, like 13. For 7 it gives 6 instead of 3.
Clearing the lowest set bit instead of the highest bit of the trailing run.
Forgetting that x = 1 has the answer 0, not -1.

complexity.time: O(n) with the bit trick, O(n · max) by trying every a

solutions.title: Try every candidate
solutions.idea: a | (a + 1) is at least a, so a < x. Test a = 0, 1, 2, … and take the first that works.

solutions.title: Clear the top bit of the trailing 1s
solutions.idea: a | (a + 1) is a with its lowest 0 switched on. So a is x with one trailing 1 cleared, and clearing the highest of them gives the smallest a.

followups: Values go up to 10^9. Which solution still works?
Return the largest valid a instead of the smallest. What changes?
